verification: Every PMID resolved through NCBI E-utilities esummary/efetch (title, first author, journal, year compared) and its abstract read; full text read where the statement depends on it (Nieman 2008 at PMC; Thornton 2013, Pivazyan 2023 and Correa 2015 via PMC/Europe PMC; NAMS 2022 PDF from menopause.org; Martin 2018 and Bornstein 2016 fetched live from academic.oup.com). Trial registrations through the ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API; FDA pages fetched live (HTTP 200); 21 CFR 310.530 through the eCFR versioner API; the Renova label and the Drugs@FDA absence check through openFDA. Nothing is included on the strength of a guide reference alone. No dose, strength or regimen from any source is reproduced. UK sources (added 2026-09-25, when Omar kept the UK in scope): legislation.gov.uk, gov.uk (MHRA, OPSS, DHSC), the electronic medicines compendium (UK SmPCs), NICE, ASA/CAP, the GPhC and the NMC fetched live and read 2026-09-25; the GMC pages and MHRA's products database were read in a browser the same day (they refuse scripts or serve no text to them).
grader: Graded 2026-09-24 by the agent under Omar Saleem's delegation ("you should be able to do that from the guide"); rule set below; final review Dr. Hannah-Shmouni
gradingRule: Grade = certainty the source gives for the specific clinical statement the lesson makes, on the guides' A–D scale. A: consistent large RCTs or approval-grade evidence. B: at least one well-designed, adequately powered RCT or an independent, quality-stratified meta-analysis (either direction). C: small or sponsor-funded RCTs without independent replication, or pooled trials dominated by them. D: animal, in-vitro, mechanistic, case series, manufacturer dossiers. 'context' = history, reviews used for framing, trial registrations without results, analytical or regulatory records (regulatory records are primary for status statements, not graded for efficacy). Where the two guides disagree, the lesson states both and the claim takes the grade the primary evidence supports. Observational studies (added 2026-09-24, GRADE starting point; confirmed by Fady Hannah-Shmouni, MD FRCPC, 2026-09-24): adequately sized cohort, case-control or cross-sectional studies grade C for the association they measured; small or single-centre ones grade D; any causal claim drawn from observational data grades D. Meta-analyses of observational studies grade at most B, and only for association. Guidelines and consensus statements are 'context', cited for what they recommend, not graded as evidence.

claims.text: Per the Endocrine Society diagnostic guideline, the features that best discriminate Cushing's syndrome are easy bruising, facial plethora, proximal myopathy and striae that are reddish-purple and wider than 1 cm; facial fullness, dorsocervical fat pad, weight gain, acne, hirsutism, thin skin and fatigue are common in the general population and less discriminatory.
claims.reviewNote: the guide's red-flag pearl matches; its 'cortisol face' description leads with less discriminating features (author finding)

claims.text: Endogenous Cushing's syndrome is uncommon (2–3 new cases per million per year in European population studies); the commonest cause of Cushing's syndrome is iatrogenic, and the guideline recommends a drug history (oral, inhaled, topical, injected — including skin-bleaching creams, herbal tonics and joint or nerve injections) before any biochemical testing.
claims.reviewNote: not stated in either guide; directly relevant to aesthetic practice

claims.text: The guideline recommends testing patients with multiple and progressive features (particularly the discriminating ones) or features unusual for age, recommends against widespread testing and against random serum cortisol, and sends abnormal results to an endocrinologist. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide adds that consumer cortisol panels are poorly validated and reads most popular 'cortisol face' as a lifestyle-and-fluid picture.

claims.text: Human skin expresses ERα, ERβ and GPR30 in aged and photoaged sites; two weeks of topical estradiol raised procollagen I/III in sun-protected hip skin of postmenopausal women but not in photoaged forearm or facial skin.

In small observational biopsy studies, skin collagen content and thickness fall by about 1–2% per year after menopause, in step with bone mass, tracking years since menopause more than chronological age. The 'up to 30% in the first five years' figure quoted by reviews and by the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide is not stated in the primary abstracts it traces to; the lesson reports it as a review figure.
claims.reviewNote: was a guide figure without a verifiable primary; rewritten as reported (m04 pattern)

claims.text: Small RCTs of systemic hormone therapy increased skin thickness (n=60, 12 months) and skin collagen (n=41, 6 months) at non-facial sites; a 2023 meta-analysis pooling small, heterogeneous studies (some non-randomized) reports higher elasticity, thickness and collagen, and its authors do not propose MHT as an independent treatment for skin ageing.

claims.text: The largest RCT of hormone therapy on facial skin (485 women, 48 weeks, low-dose) found no significant difference from placebo in wrinkling or sagging, and a 4-year randomized study in recently menopausal women (KEEPS) found no difference in wrinkle or rigidity scores. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide grades the skin benefit B; the NAMS 2022 statement rates its skin key point Level II (limited or inconsistent); the course grades the structural effects C and states that a visible wrinkle benefit has not been shown in the largest trials.

claims.text: In the US (FDA request of 10 Nov 2025; first approved labels 12 Feb 2026), approved uses of menopausal hormone therapy are moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms, vulvovaginal/genitourinary symptoms and, for some products, prevention of bone loss; the labeling changes removed cardiovascular, breast-cancer and probable-dementia statements from the boxed warning and did not add skin as an indication.
claims.reviewNote: US only; absent from both guides

claims.text: The NAMS 2022 position statement finds the benefit–risk ratio favourable for bothersome VMS and prevention of bone loss in women under 60 or within 10 years of menopause without contraindications, and finds insufficient evidence and safety concerns for compounded bioidentical hormone therapy (patient preference alone should not justify it); WHI findings do not support MHT for chronic disease prevention. Skin benefit is secondary and never on its own an indication (Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide).
claims.gradeDecision: guideline records + A (WHI); the 'never an indication' boundary is the guide's position

claims.text: Low-dose vaginal estrogen is effective for moderate-to-severe genitourinary syndrome of menopause without an added progestogen — the one setting where estrogen is given for the tissue itself.

Skin-directed care with stronger evidence: daily broad-spectrum sunscreen reduced measured skin ageing over 4.5 years in a 903-person independent RCT, and in the US one tretinoin cream is FDA-approved as an adjunct for mitigating fine facial wrinkles (its label states it does not eliminate wrinkles or reverse photoaging).
claims.reviewNote: the guide's menopause algorithm lists retinoids (A) and daily sunscreen
claims.gradeDecision: B (sunscreen RCT); approval-grade for the adjunct fine-wrinkle label

claims.text: In a consecutive NIH series of 32 people with MEN1, 88% had multiple facial angiofibromas (identical to those of tuberous sclerosis) and 72% collagenomas; angiofibromas outside tuberous sclerosis warrant biochemical testing for MEN1.

Carney complex (over 70% carry inactivating PRKAR1A variants) presents with lentigines typically on the face, lips and mucosa (canthal pigmentation is seen only in Carney complex and Peutz–Jeghers syndrome), blue naevi and cutaneous myxomas (eyelid, ear, nipple); cardiac myxomas occur in 20–40% and cause more than half of disease mortality, which is why early detection and echocardiographic screening matter.
claims.reviewNote: the guide's Carney entry omits cardiac myxomas (author finding)
claims.gradeDecision: context — clinical review by the leading group

claims.text: In MEN2A, cutaneous lichen amyloidosis — most often over the scapular upper back — clusters with RET codon-634 variants and is typically detected before medullary thyroid cancer.

Primary adrenal insufficiency causes hyperpigmentation particularly of sun-exposed areas, skin creases, mucosa and scars; the Endocrine Society recommends testing acutely ill patients with such signs and treating a suspected adrenal crisis before test results are available.

A rapid pace or progression of hirsutism, or virilization (clitoromegaly, deepening voice, increasing muscularity), points to a greater likelihood of an androgen-secreting neoplasm (about 0.2% of hyperandrogenic women; over half malignant); the Endocrine Society suggests against androgen testing in women with regular cycles and unwanted local hair without an abnormal hirsutism score.
claims.reviewNote: matches the guide's acne/androgen algorithm ('rapid virilization demands urgent work-up')

claims.text: Other common endocrine skin signs: acanthosis nigricans tracks hyperinsulinaemia and insulin resistance; pretibial myxoedema reflects thyrotropin-receptor stimulation in Graves' disease; cold, dry skin suggests hypothyroidism.

In the UK (product information checked 25 September 2026), HRT products such as estradiol patches (Evorel) and gel (Sandrena) are prescription-only medicines licensed for oestrogen-deficiency symptoms in peri- and postmenopausal women and, for some presentations, for preventing osteoporosis in postmenopausal women at high risk of fracture who cannot take other medicines approved for it; skin is not among their licensed uses.
claims.reviewNote: UK mapping added 2026-09-25 (Omar kept the UK in scope); confirmation pending with the post-approval changes

claims.text: In the UK, a hormone preparation compounded in a pharmacy or made as a 'special' is an unlicensed medicine; MHRA guidance says an unlicensed product should not be supplied where a licensed product can meet the patient's need, and a UK-licensed product used off-label comes before an unlicensed one.
claims.reviewNote: UK mapping added 2026-09-25 (Omar kept the UK in scope); confirmation pending with the post-approval changes

claims.text: On the UK electronic medicines compendium (searched 25 September 2026), topical tretinoin appears only in acne treatments: Treclin gel (clindamycin with tretinoin) and Aknemycin Plus (erythromycin with tretinoin); the other tretinoin product listed is an oral capsule.
claims.reviewNote: UK mapping added 2026-09-25 (Omar kept the UK in scope); confirmation pending with the post-approval changes

authorFindings: A&RE ch.9 — 'skin collagen falls … on the order of 30% within the first five years, then roughly 2% per year' (refs 1 and 3, both reviews). The primary biopsy studies it traces to report 1–2% a year tracking years since menopause (Brincat 1985, PMID 3978054; Brincat 1987, PMID 3120067; Affinito 1999, PMID 10656502); none of their abstracts states the 30% figure, which appears in reviews (e.g., Thornton 2013). The course teaches 1–2% a year and names 30% as a review figure. Suggest citing the primary study that reports it, or dropping it.

A&RE ch.9 grades the skin effect of MHT GRADE B, citing the NAMS 2022 statement. NAMS itself rates that key point Level II (limited or inconsistent) on the strength of one review. The largest RCT of HT on facial skin (Phillips 2008, n=485, PMID 18625536) and the 4-year KEEPS skin study (Owen 2016, PMID 27393520) found no difference in wrinkles; neither is cited by the guide. The course grades structural effects (thickness, collagen) C and says a visible wrinkle benefit has not been shown in the largest trials. The guide may wish to revisit B.

A&RE ch.9 ref 8 (Pivazyan 2023) — pools small, heterogeneous studies including non-randomized ones (I² 64–98%), omits KEEPS, and its own authors say MHT should not be considered an independent treatment for skin ageing. Suggest describing it as low-certainty support.

A&RE ch.8 'cortisol face' — the opening description of the 'genuine endocrine entity' leads with moon facies and dorsocervical/supraclavicular fat pads, which the Endocrine Society guideline (Nieman 2008, Table 1) lists among common, less discriminatory features; its best discriminators are easy bruising, facial plethora, proximal myopathy and reddish-purple striae >1 cm. The chapter's clinical pearl already lists the right red flags; suggest the description lead with them.

A&RE ch.8 — worth adding the guideline's first step: a drug history for exogenous glucocorticoids, including topical and skin-bleaching creams, herbal tonics and joint or nerve injections (Nieman 2008, 3.1), since iatrogenic Cushing's is the commonest form and the most relevant to aesthetic practice.

A&RE inherited-syndromes chapter — the Carney complex entry omits cardiac myxomas, present in 20–40% of patients and responsible for more than half of disease mortality (Correa 2015, PMID 26130139). They are the main reason a lentigines-plus-myxoma pattern is a referral. PRKAR1A '~70%' matches Correa 2015 ('more than 70%').

A&RE ch.9 — 'topical estrogen creams … are absorbed systemically' is not stated in the cited review's abstract (Shu & Maibach 2011) and was not verified; the course teaches the US regulatory position instead (21 CFR 310.530: an OTC 'hormone cream' is an unapproved new drug).

A&RE ch.9 and ch.14 — FDA's menopausal hormone therapy labeling action (request 10 Nov 2025; first six approved labels 12 Feb 2026: cardiovascular, breast-cancer and probable-dementia statements removed from the boxed warning) is not mentioned. Suggest adding it, date-stamped, because it changes how the risk conversation is framed; approved indications did not change and do not include skin.

A&RE algorithms pp.93–96 are images only; the course used them to locate claims and sourced every teaching statement to a primary or guideline record. The menopause algorithm's 'topical estrogen off-label (C)' box would read more safely as 'not recommended for wrinkles' to match ch.9's text.

All other A&RE ch.8, ch.9 and inherited-syndrome references resolved on PubMed with matching title, first author, journal and year (Slominski 2000, Tiganescu 2011, Schoepe 2006, Nieman 2008, Hall 2005, Thornton 2013, Brincat 2005, NAMS 2022 and 2020, Shu 2011, Manson 2013, Pivazyan 2023, Lause 2017, Darling 1997, Stanescu 2024, Kirschner 2000).

Not in either guide, worth adding — Ajjan 2022 (first human RCT of 11β-HSD1 inhibition in skin; pilot, primary outcome missed), Phillips 2008 and Owen 2016 (negative HT wrinkle trials), Martin 2018 (Endocrine Society hirsutism guideline: rapid progression or virilization → androgen-secreting tumour, ~0.2%, over half malignant), Bornstein 2016 (hyperpigmentation distribution in primary adrenal insufficiency), Correa 2015 (Carney complex cardiac myxomas), Hughes 2013 (sunscreen RCT, n=903) and the Renova label (the one FDA-approved adjunct for fine facial wrinkles).

UK status (2026-09-25) — neither guide gives a UK position for menopausal hormone therapy or tretinoin. UK HRT licences (e.g. Evorel patches, Sandrena gel) cover oestrogen-deficiency symptoms and, for some products, osteoporosis prevention; a compounded 'bioidentical' preparation is an unlicensed medicine in the UK (MHRA Guidance Note 14 places any licensed product that meets the need first). The UK medicines compendium lists topical tretinoin only in acne combinations (Treclin, Aknemycin Plus), so the guides' 'prescription retinoid for photoageing' advice reads as US practice for a UK reader. MHRA's products database could not confirm an absence for tretinoin (its full-text search returns 289 documents), so the course states only what the compendium lists.
